newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia lacks funds for AIDS prevention - official.
newsitem.headline: Russia lacks funds for AIDS prevention - official.

text.p: A lack of cash is thwarting efforts to raise awareness of the acute danger posed to Russia by the spread of AIDS, a health ministry official said on Thursday.
The government has not distributed any of the funds it designated for AIDS prevention programmes this year, said Alexander Galiysov, a specialist in the ministry's AIDS prevention department.
"We have not received any money from the state budget this year except for medicines to diagnose and treat infected patients," he said by telephone.
This left local authorities and volunteers with the mammoth task of persuading Russians through information campaigns that AIDS (Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome) was a real danger.
"All the rest comes from pure enthusiasm and money from local budgets," Galiysov said.
Russia's relative isolation under communism and government restrictions on sexual behaviour and drug abuse contained the spread of AIDS until 1991.
Consequently, many Russians still see it as a disease that afflicts only foreigners and measures have been focused on the perceived threat from outside.
Parliament passed a law last year requiring visitors applying for long-term visas to prove they did not have the human immuno-deficiency (HIV) virus which causes AIDS.

The law has not been implemented but the threat of AIDS within Russia has also been neglected. The 1996 budget for anti-AIDS measures, theoretically 69.9 billion roubles ($13.9 million), has been more than halved in next year's draft budget.
The official figures are still small by international standards -- 2,081 people reported HIV-positive and 245 with the full-blown disease among a population of 150 million.
But 60 people are estimated to get infected each day and a dramatic rise in other sexually-transmitted diseases heralds a greater growth in numbers.
Mikhail Narkevich, a coordinator of Russia's AIDS control programme, said on Tuesday the country faced an AIDS epidemic.

Russia's anti-AIDS programme involves establishing a legal base for the fight against AIDS, information campaigns, improved health checks, guranteeing the safety of blood donations and improving diagnostics and training.

Galiysov said condoms -- widely seen as a joke under communism -- would be distributed in Moscow and St Petersburg for World AIDS Day on Sunday and a concert would be held in Moscow to raise awareness of the disease.
Private condom manufacturers said they would also distribute condoms in other Russian towns.
Galiysov said his department had not given up hope that some funds might come its way. "The year is not over yet. Maybe we will get something in December," he added.
